summary: Defines a MIB module for managing pseudowire edge-to-edge services carried over a general packet switched network, giving network management tools a standard way to model and monitor them.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire is a pretend cable across a network. This is a list of dials and gauges that lets managers check on the pretend cable.

questions: how to manage pseudowires with snmp
what tables are in the pw mib
subtitle: A standard SNMP data model for configuring and monitoring pseudowires, the emulated circuits carried across a packet network.

tldr.problem: Operators who run pseudowire services over a packet switched network need a common way to configure and monitor them from network management tools, whatever service or network type is involved.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5601 defines the PW-STD-MIB module, with a main pwTable for generic configuration and status, three performance tables, and two reverse-mapping tables. It also defines the IANA-PWE3-MIB module for PW type and PSN type values.
tldr.outcome: Service-specific and PSN-specific MIB modules attach to the same pwIndex, so one generic module serves every pseudowire type. Managing the objects needs SNMPv3 security.

today: RFC 5601 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the PW MIB Covers
sections.content:
RFC 5601 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing pseudowire (PW) services that travel over a Packet Switched Network (PSN). It covers the generic management that is common to all types of PSN and to all PW services defined by the IETF PWE3 Working Group.

As with other MIBs, the objects are normally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) and are written in SMIv2, the Structure of Management Information described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a standard menu of settings and readings for pretend cables, so every manager and every box speak the same language.

sections.title: A Layered Set of MIB Modules
sections.content:
The PWE3 MIB architecture is a layered, modular model. Any supported emulated service can be connected to any supported PSN type. Defining a PW therefore takes at least three kinds of MIB module:

  • A service-specific module, which depends on the emulated signal type and is defined in other documents.
  • The PW-STD-MIB module defined here, which configures the general parameters that are common to all emulated services and PSN types. It is the glue that maps the emulated service onto the native PSN service.
  • A PSN-specific module, one for each PSN type, which associates the PW with one or more tunnels that carry the service. RFC 5602 is given as an example.

A row in a service-specific or PSN-specific module is linked to the main table by the common pwIndex.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of three stacked building blocks: one for what is being carried, one in the middle for the shared settings, and one for the road it travels on. They click together using the same number.

sections.title: The Tables of PW-STD-MIB
sections.content:
The module consists of six tables:

  • pwTable: generic configuration and status objects common to all service and PSN types.
  • pwPerfCurrentTable: statistics for the current 15-minute period.
  • pwPerfIntervalTable: statistics for historical intervals, usually 96 entries of 15 minutes to cover 24 hours.
  • pwPerf1DayIntervalTable: statistics accumulated per day, usually 30 entries to cover a month.
  • pwIndexMappingTable: reverse mapping from the unique PW identity (peer IP, PW type and PW ID) to the pwIndex.
  • pwGenFecIndexMappingTable: the same reverse mapping for the identifiers used with generic FEC signaling (group, local and peer attachment IDs).

The module reuses textual conventions from several other RFCs, including the PW textual conventions of RFC 5542.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one big form for each pretend cable, a few score sheets that keep its recent results, and two phone books for finding a cable from its details.

sections.title: Creating and Using PW Rows
sections.content:
An entry in pwTable MUST exist for every PW type (ATM, FR, Ethernet, SONET and so on). A row can come about in three ways:

  • The operator creates it while configuring a new service. Agents MUST support this, and it MUST be used for non-signaled (manually assigned) PWs.
  • The agent MAY create it when a signaling message arrives from a peer with identification parameters not already known locally. This is optional.
  • The agent MAY create it from an auto-discovery application or from configuration done outside SNMP. This is also optional.

The agent then creates the matching rows in the performance and reverse-mapping tables it supports. Rows in the PSN-specific and service-specific modules are tied to the PW by the shared pwIndex. Until all required entries exist and are consistently configured, signaling cannot start from the local node and pwVcOperStatus should report notPresent.

RFC 5601 includes a worked example of a Circuit Emulation over Packet (CEP) PW over an MPLS tunnel, signaled with LDP as in RFC 4447. The example sets values such as pwIndex 5, pwID 10 and pwLocalGroupID 12, and is continued in the service-specific and MPLS module documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Usually a person fills in the form to make a new pretend cable. Sometimes the box fills in a form by itself when a neighbor asks for one.

sections.title: Relation to IF-MIB and Notifications
sections.content:
A PW is generally not an ifIndex on its own, for agent scalability reasons. It is normally associated with the ifIndex it emulates, such as a SONET path for CEP or a virtual interface for a VPLS bridge. Some implementations may find it convenient to manage the PW as an ifIndex; in that case the special ifType 246 is used and, by default, the PW SHOULD NOT be stacked above the PSN tunnel or attachment circuit interfaces.

The module has notifications for a PW entering the up or down state, following the interface notification guidelines of RFC 2863. Implementers are told that many systems correlate notifications so that none is sent when a higher layer (a port or tunnel) has already reported. When a PW is represented as an ifIndex, it is RECOMMENDED that PW notifications be turned off to avoid duplicating the ifIndex status change notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the time the pretend cable is not given its own interface slot. If it is, the alarms should ring once, not twice.

sections.title: IANA-PWE3-MIB and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
The document includes the initial IANA-PWE3-MIB module, which defines three textual conventions: IANAPwTypeTC (the carried service, for example Ethernet, ATM, PPP and CEP), IANAPwPsnTypeTC (the PSN type, with values such as MPLS, L2TP and MPLS over GRE) and IANAPwCapabilities (a set of bits such as status indication and VCCV). New PW types and PSN types are added by IANA following expert review under RFC 4446.

IANA assigned ifType value 246 for a PW. The pwStdMIB identifier sits under the transmission subtree because a PW may appear as an ifIndex; other PW-related MIB modules SHOULD be assigned under mib-2.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared sticker book lists the kinds of pretend cables and the kinds of roads. A librarian adds new stickers when needed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module can configure as well as monitor, and anything configurable can be misconfigured with potentially disastrous results. pwTable holds the settings for a Provider Edge (PE) device, so unauthorized access could disrupt traffic. The objects pwUpDownNotifEnable and pwNotifRate control status reports, and tampering could give operators a wrong view of the network.

Readable objects can also be sensitive, because the tables together show the PW topology and its performance. The RFC says SNMPv3 VACM and USM MUST be used with any v3 agent implementing this module, recommends SNMPv3 with cryptographic security, and says deploying SNMP versions before v3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: The dials can break things if the wrong person turns them, and the gauges tell secrets about your network. So lock the control room and only let trusted people in.
